article.headline: Citrini's Three-Year AI Trade: 400% Return, One Pivotal Short
article.lede: CitriniResearch's Dynamic AI portfolio crossed +400% total return in May 2026, roughly three years after its May 2023 inception, against approximately 254% for the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, the sector's standard benchmark. The portfolio's 46 holdings rotated systematically through AI infrastructure sub-themes — GPUs, optical networking, advanced packaging, power, and chip testing — as each layer hit its valuation peak. Its single largest contributor was not a long position but a short on that benchmark, placed the Friday before DeepSeek's January 2025 market shock.
article.body:
The portfolio operated on a rotating *picks-and-shovels* thesis — buying infrastructure layers rather than AI end-applications, then moving capital as each layer hit its valuation peak or supply bottleneck. Over 46 disclosed holdings across roughly a thousand days, CitriniResearch worked systematically through the supply chain: GPU server assembly (Celestica (CLS), Amkor Technology (AMKR)), optical networking (Credo Technology (CRDO), Ciena (CIEN)), chip testing equipment (Aehr Test Systems (AEHR)), and data-center power and cooling (Vertiv Holdings (VRT)), alongside materials firms that most generalist investors had never heard of.

Among the long contributors, Soitec (SOI FP) and Unimicron Technology (3037 TT) exemplify the granularity of the approach. Soitec, a French wafer-materials company, is the dominant producer of Photonics-SOI substrate — the engineered silicon platform underlying *silicon photonics*, the optical-interconnect technology linking dense GPU clusters at data-center scale. Unimicron occupies an equally narrow chokepoint: *ABF (Ajinomoto Build-up Film) substrates*, the precision bonding layers between advanced AI chips and their circuit boards in modern server packaging; alongside Japan's Ibiden (4062 JP), the two effectively form a duopoly on materials that no leading-edge GPU package can be built without. Vertiv Holdings (VRT) supplies the power distribution and liquid-cooling systems that high-density GPU racks — running at 40–130 kilowatts each, versus five to ten for conventional servers — require. Aehr Test Systems (AEHR) makes the *wafer-level burn-in* equipment that stress-tests AI chips before packaging, catching infant-failure defects that would otherwise surface as outages in always-on infrastructure.

**The single largest contributor** — +26.8 percentage points of total return — was not a long but a short on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), the 25-stock sector benchmark heavily weighted toward Nvidia (NVDA). On January 24, 2025, Citrini published analysis concluding that DeepSeek's new reasoning model — trained on a reported budget of roughly $6 million, a fraction of Western lab costs — would be “extremely bearish for *Phase 1* hardware demand” and pivoted roughly half the portfolio to the SMH short. Three days later, Nvidia shed approximately $589 billion in market capitalization in a single session — the largest single-day market-cap loss in U.S. stock-market history — and SMH fell 9.8%, its worst day in nearly five years. The position was covered in April 2025. The trade was not a repudiation of the AI bull thesis but a precise application of it: two years of supply-chain mapping allowed Citrini to identify that efficient open-source training threatened the specific bottleneck — premium-priced GPU shipments — on which the market was most concentrated.

Among the longest-held positions, MACOM Technology Solutions (MTSI) — a designer of high-speed analog and photonics ICs used in 800G and 1.6T data-center *optical transceivers* — is shown with a +2,993% total return over a 786-day holding period. MACOM's published three-year stock-price return is approximately 510%, a strong result but well below the disclosed figure; the gap likely reflects either a leveraged or options-based position, an unusually low average cost basis, or an OCR misread of the source chart. The underlying thesis is well-grounded: Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue rose 22.5% year-on-year, driven by demand for MACOM's photonics drivers in high-speed data-center interconnects.

The tweet's closing observation carries its own weight: across more than a thousand days, Citrini reports that not one passed without someone calling the AI infrastructure trade a bubble. SMH itself — despite the DeepSeek selloff and multiple 20–30% drawdowns — returned roughly 254% over the same window, evidence that the underlying hardware demand was real even when valuations ran ahead of it. What the Dynamic AI portfolio's 400%-plus record suggests is that a thematic investor who maps a supply chain thoroughly enough to spot its bottlenecks on the way up can also identify the moment the market has priced those bottlenecks to perfection — and that shorting the benchmark at that point is not a change of thesis but a sharper expression of it.

concepts.definition: An investing strategy that targets the tools, materials, and infrastructure enabling a technology wave rather than the end-applications themselves. The name alludes to the California Gold Rush, where suppliers of equipment profited more reliably than most prospectors. In AI, it means buying semiconductor equipment, packaging substrates, power components, and networking hardware rather than AI software firms.

A technology for transmitting data as pulses of light on silicon chips rather than as electrical signals over copper wires. Inside AI data centers, silicon photonics enables the high-bandwidth, low-latency links between GPU clusters that copper interconnects cannot support at scale. It depends on specialized engineered wafer substrates — such as Soitec's Photonics-SOI — as its material platform.

ABF stands for Ajinomoto Build-up Film, a laminated resin material that forms the micro-circuit layers in high-performance chip packages. These substrates electrically connect an advanced processor die to its circuit board with nanometer-scale precision and are a critical bottleneck in the production of GPUs and AI accelerators. Only a handful of firms worldwide — principally Unimicron and Ibiden — can manufacture them at the required quality for leading-edge chips.

A reliability-screening step in which semiconductor wafers are subjected to elevated heat and voltage stress before being diced and packaged, triggering early-life failures — sometimes called 'infant mortality' failures — while they are still inexpensive to discard. For high-uptime AI accelerators, catching these failures before packaging is far cheaper than field replacements. Aehr Test Systems is the primary vendor of this equipment for the AI chip market.

CitriniResearch's label for the first wave of AI investment: the hardware and infrastructure buildout — GPUs, memory, networking, advanced packaging, and power — that preceded the application-layer software wave. The framework held that investors should identify and rotate into each successive hardware bottleneck, then exit to 'Phase 2' software and deployment names once market pricing had fully absorbed each bottleneck thesis.

A module that converts electrical signals into light pulses and back, enabling high-speed data transmission over fiber-optic cables. In AI data centers, 800G and 1.6T transceivers connect switch-to-GPU and rack-to-rack links at speeds that copper cables cannot economically match at distance. MACOM Technology Solutions supplies the high-speed analog driver ICs that power these modules.

article.fact_check: The +2,993% total return attributed to MACOM Technology Solutions (MTSI) over a 786-day holding period cannot be reconciled with publicly available price data. MACOM's three-year stock-price return is approximately 510% as of May 2026 — a strong result, but far below the disclosed figure. The most probable explanations are: (1) the position was held via options or another leveraged instrument, multiplying the underlying stock move; (2) the realized-return calculation used an average cost basis established at a price well below the May 2023 inception date; or (3) the figure is an OCR artefact of the source chart image, where a number such as 299.3% could plausibly be misread as 2,993%. The brief presents the figure with this caveat; readers should not treat it as a verified equity-only return.

ticker_cls.description: Celestica is a Canadian EMS (Electronics Manufacturing Services) company that has rapidly become one of the leading contract manufacturers for AI infrastructure — assembling AI servers, networking switches, storage arrays, and hardware platform solutions for hyperscale data center operators. Its Connectivity and Cloud segment grew 76% year-over-year in Q1 2026. Q1 2026 revenue of $4.05 billion (+53% YoY) drove management to raise full-year 2026 guidance to $17 billion with $8.75 adjusted EPS. The company is expanding capacity in Thailand and building a major new Texas facility.

ticker_amkr.description: Amkor Technology is the largest Western-headquartered OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test) provider, packaging finished silicon dies into the chips that power AI accelerators, smartphones, and automotive systems. The company is investing heavily in advanced packaging technologies — 2.5D, 3D stacking, and flip-chip — and is building a major domestic facility in Peoria, Arizona as part of the U.S. semiconductor reshoring effort. Q1 2026 revenue hit $1.685 billion (+27% YoY), with management guiding that its AI packaging portfolio would triple in the second half of 2026.

ticker_crdo.blurb: Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd is a semiconductor company that provides high-speed, low-power connectivity solutions for data centers and AI infrastructure. Its key products include the Pilot software platform and ZeroFlap optical transceivers, which are increasingly adopted by hyperscalers. The company is emerging as a critical enabler of AI infrastructure, addressing bandwidth bottlenecks in high-performance computing.
ticker_crdo.recent: In the past 30 days, Credo reported record third-quarter FY26 results, driven by growing hyperscaler adoption of its Pilot platform and ZeroFlap optical transceivers. The company also presented its connectivity innovations at TSMC’s 2026 North America Technology Symposium. Its stock has been volatile amid broader AI infrastructure demand trends.

ticker_aehr.name: Aehr Test Systems
ticker_aehr.blurb: Aehr Test Systems designs and manufactures wafer-level burn-in and test equipment for semiconductors, with a specialisation in silicon carbide (SiC) power devices, gallium nitride (GaN), and — increasingly — silicon photonics chips. Its flagship FOX-XP system stress-tests devices while still on the wafer, before costly packaging, identifying failures at the cheapest possible point in manufacturing. Aehr claims to be the first company to ship a multi-wafer burn-in solution for silicon photonics transceivers. The company is headquartered in Fremont, California.
ticker_aehr.recent: In March 2026, Aehr won a new silicon photonics customer for its high-power FOX-XP wafer-level burn-in system targeting hyperscale data-centre optical interconnects. Quarterly bookings reached $37.2 million in the quarter ending February 2026 — a book-to-bill ratio exceeding 3.5x — with the company guiding full-year FY2026 revenue toward the high end of its $45–$50 million range. Revenue in the same quarter was $10.3 million, down from $18.3 million a year earlier, reflecting a timing gap between order intake and shipment schedules weighted toward the second half of 2026.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

poster_citrini.blurb: Independent thematic-equity research firm founded in 2023 by James van Geelen, a self-taught investor who began his career in alternative healthcare before turning to public markets in 2018. Citrini publishes via paid Substack, runs a portfolio of long/short thematic baskets called the Citrindex, and has built a following on X for early calls on AI 'picks and shovels,' GLP-1 obesity drugs, and idiosyncratic trades such as a public short of Silicon Valley Bank in late 2022, months before its collapse. The firm now reports roughly ten employees and covers themes spanning AI, robotics, defence, healthcare and government policy.
poster_citrini.credibility_note: Track-record claims are largely self-reported through paywalled subscriber notes; the firm's '+131% since inception' and '+100% one-year' figures for its core portfolio cannot be audited externally. That said, several specific calls have been corroborated in the public press: the early 2023 AI hardware basket, the SVB short, and a February 2026 note on AI capex sustainability that was credited by Bloomberg with helping trigger an equity-market sell-off. Van Geelen, born around 1992, holds bachelor's degrees in biology and psychology from UCLA and is not a CFA charterholder; positions described in Citrini notes are the firm's own, and readers should assume the firm transacts in the names it covers.
